strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: unifying motion synthesis and comprehension across text, audio, single-person, and two-person motion tasks in one autoregressive LLM-style framework. The breadth of supported tasks is substantially larger than most prior motion LLM systems.

MotionHub is a potentially valuable contribution. Aggregating, normalizing, filtering, and re-captioning many public motion datasets into a multimodal multitask resource could be useful to the community, especially for full-body and dual-person motion modeling.

The HoMi tokenizer is a technically sensible component. The separation of body and hand encoders plus frequency-aware gating is well motivated, and the ablations show clear reconstruction improvements over simpler single-codebook variants.

Experimental coverage is broad. The paper reports results for text-to-motion, motion-to-text, interaction motion, motion completion/in-betweening, music-to-dance, dance-to-music, speech-to-gesture, and tokenizer reconstruction, which supports the central claim of a general framework.

Some results are convincing: motion-to-text and interaction motion-to-text improve over baselines on most metrics, motion completion/in-betweening is competitive or better, and the tokenizer reconstruction results are strong relative to single-codebook alternatives and close to RVQ.
weaknesses: The empirical case is uneven. On single-person text-to-motion, MotionLLaMA is not the best method and trails several specialized baselines in R-Precision, FID, and MM-Dist. On AIST++ music-to-dance, its FIDk is much worse than prior methods. On speech-to-gesture, FGD and diversity are worse than strong baselines, despite good beat alignment. The paper’s SOTA language sometimes overstates these mixed results.

Fairness and reproducibility of the evaluation are not fully established. Many baselines appear to be reimplemented or retrained on MotionHub, but the paper gives limited detail on splits, hyperparameter parity, checkpoint selection, and whether any source datasets overlap between training and evaluation in ways that could affect comparisons.

The dataset contribution needs stronger documentation. The paper relies on manual filtering and GPT-4o recaptioning/rewriting, but does not provide enough information about annotation protocol, quality control, inter-annotator agreement, caption validation, or licensing/redistribution constraints for the aggregated public datasets.

The method’s conceptual novelty is moderate. The overall recipe, discrete motion/audio tokenizers plus LLM fine-tuning with special tokens and LoRA, follows existing multimodal LLM and motion-tokenizer paradigms. The strongest novelty is engineering breadth and dataset scale rather than a fundamentally new modeling principle.

Some task evaluations are narrow. Dance-to-music is evaluated mainly by beat coverage/hit metrics, which do not measure musical quality, style, or perceptual plausibility. Motion generation results rely heavily on embedding-based metrics and limited visual examples; user studies or physical plausibility/contact analyses would strengthen the claims.

Several presentation issues reduce confidence: inconsistent MotionHub counts between the abstract/contributions and supplementary table, OCR-visible figure/text rendering problems around Fig. 4, typos such as “instruction-truing” and “Texst-to-Motion,” and occasional imprecise claims such as codebook-size discussion written as 2^11/2^9 but extracted ambiguously as 211/29.

strengths: The paper targets an ambitious and relevant problem: unifying motion synthesis and comprehension across text, motion, music, speech, single-person motion, and two-person interaction. This breadth is a meaningful systems contribution if adequately supported.

The MotionHub aggregation is potentially useful: it standardizes multiple public motion datasets, includes single-person and two-person data, and provides paired text/audio supervision for several tasks.

The HoMi tokenizer is a plausible technical component. The separation of body and hand encoders plus frequency-aware gating is motivated, and the reconstruction tables show strong results versus single-codebook baselines and comparable results to RVQ on several metrics.

The manuscript includes evaluations over many tasks rather than only demonstrating one favored setting, and some results are positive, especially motion-to-text, interaction motion-to-text, motion completion/in-betweening, dance-to-music beat metrics, and tokenizer reconstruction.
weaknesses: The empirical case does not justify the broad SOTA framing. On text-to-motion, MotionLLaMA is worse than several baselines on R-Precision, FID, and MM distance; on AIST++ music-to-dance its FID is much worse than all listed baselines; on speech-to-gesture its FGD is worse than MCM and DiffStyleGesture and its diversity is below real data. These mixed results conflict with the strong claims in the abstract and conclusion.

The evaluation protocol is insufficiently clear and may favor the proposed benchmark. MotionHub is both the training corpus and the basis for several re-run evaluations, and the paper gives little detail on train/validation/test splits, overlap control across aggregated datasets, or whether captions/motions from related sources leak between training and evaluation.

Several metrics depend on feature extractors trained by the authors on MotionHub, including TMR variants and gesture VAE features. This may be reasonable, but without independent validation or public standardized protocols, the reported improvements are difficult to interpret and compare fairly to prior work.

The main method is mostly an assembly of existing ingredients: VQ-VAE-style motion tokenization, WavTokenizer, LLaMA-3.2 with LoRA, and prompt-based multitask tuning. The paper does not clearly isolate what is novel beyond engineering integration, and the ablations are narrow, focusing mainly on reconstruction rather than downstream task impact.

The dataset contribution is under-documented. The manuscript says data were manually filtered, annotated, and recaptioned with ChatGPT-4o, but gives little information about annotator guidelines, quality control, inter-annotator agreement, licensing constraints, consent/privacy considerations, or error analysis of rewritten captions.

There is no human evaluation or perceptual study despite the output modalities being motion, gesture, dance, and music, where automatic metrics are known to be incomplete. The authors even note a limitation of BAS, but still rely heavily on automatic metrics, including a dance-to-music result with perfect beat coverage that warrants qualitative scrutiny.

Reproducibility details are weak for a large systems paper. Compute budget, batch sizes, sequence lengths, model size/variant specifics, data splits, sampling details, preprocessing code, and baseline retraining settings are not described sufficiently to reproduce the results.

The presentation has many rough spots: typos such as 'Texst-to-Motion' and 'instruction-truing', garbled Figure 4 text extraction/appearance, inconsistent task counts, and some unclear claims about codebook size/utilization. These issues do not by themselves determine rejection, but they reinforce concern that the technical case has not been carefully communicated.

strengths: The paper tackles an ambitious and timely problem: a unified LLM-based framework for both motion synthesis and motion comprehension across many motion-centric tasks, including single-person, two-person interaction, audio-conditioned generation, motion completion, and bidirectional text/motion or dance/music tasks. This breadth is a meaningful contribution for ECCV if the released code and MotionHub data are usable.

The HoMi tokenizer is technically well motivated. Separating body and hand encoders while keeping a single codebook is a sensible design for full-body motion, and the reconstruction experiments show strong gains over single-codebook VQ baselines and performance close to or slightly better than RVQ on several body/global metrics.

The dataset engineering contribution is substantial. MotionHub aggregates many public sources, standardizes SMPL-family representations, adds/normalizes captions, includes both single- and dual-person data, and supports multiple modalities. This is valuable beyond the particular model.

The experimental coverage is unusually broad. The paper evaluates text-to-motion, motion-to-text, interaction text-to-motion, interaction motion-to-text, motion completion/in-betweening, music-to-dance, dance-to-music, speech-to-gesture, and tokenizer reconstruction, with comparisons to relevant prior methods in each area.

Results are convincing on several tasks: motion-to-text and interaction motion-to-text improve over prior methods on most metrics, interaction text-to-motion shows strong alignment gains, motion completion/in-betweening improves ADE/FDE, and dance-to-music reports clear gains on beat metrics.
The paper includes useful ablations for the tokenizer components, motion representation, and codebook size, supporting the core design choices rather than presenting the architecture as a black box.
weaknesses: The empirical case is uneven across tasks. For single-person text-to-motion, MotionLLaMA is not state of the art on R-Precision, FID, or multimodal distance; for AIST++ music-to-dance, its FIDk is much worse than several baselines; and for speech-to-gesture, FGD is worse than MCM and L1Div is not competitive. The paper sometimes frames these results more strongly than the numbers justify.

Fairness of comparisons is not fully resolved. MotionLLaMA uses a large LLaMA-3.2 backbone and a large curated multitask dataset, while several baselines appear to be retrained or evaluated under different capacities and task scopes. The paper would benefit from clearer compute/model-size reporting, identical training-data protocols, and stronger discussion of whether gains come from architecture, scale, data, or tokenizer quality.

The MotionHub construction is valuable but underdocumented for reproducibility and auditability. The manuscript gives high-level filtering and ChatGPT-based recaptioning steps, but lacks enough detail on annotation guidelines, quality control, train/test split construction, possible overlap among source datasets, and safeguards against caption or motion leakage across evaluation splits.

Several evaluation metrics are imperfect for the claimed capabilities. Dance-to-music relies mainly on beat coverage/hit/F1, which may not reflect musical quality; the paper even notes BAS limitations for music-to-dance. Human studies, perceptual evaluation, or stronger semantic/audio quality metrics would make the multimodal generation claims more persuasive.

The LLM training recipe is still somewhat underspecified despite many implementation details. For example, the exact task mixtures, prompt templates, token sequence formats, maximum sequence lengths, training compute, and expert-vs-unified model usage in each table are not always clear enough for independent reproduction.

The method’s originality is solid but partly incremental: it combines known ingredients, including VQ-style motion tokenization, WavTokenizer, LoRA-tuned LLaMA, prompt-based multitask learning, and dataset aggregation. The main novelty lies in the integrated system, HoMi design, and dataset scale rather than a fundamentally new generative modeling principle.

Limitations and societal impact are minimal. Given the use of generated human motion, speech/gesture data, LLM-generated captions, and possible downstream use in animation or synthetic humans, more discussion of biases, consent/licensing of aggregated datasets, misuse, and failure modes would strengthen the submission.
